title: Why Deserts Get Cold at Night
subject: geo
paras: Many people imagine deserts as places that are hot all the time. In fact, some deserts are among the coldest places on Earth at night. In the Sahara, the temperature can rise above 40°C during the day and fall close to freezing a few hours after sunset. This large daily range is one of the most typical features of desert climates.

The main reason is the lack of water. Water vapor in the air acts like a blanket. During the day it absorbs some of the sun's energy, and at night it traps heat near the ground. Desert air is very dry, so there is little vapor to hold the heat. As soon as the sun goes down, the heat that the ground collected during the day escapes quickly into space.

Clouds also matter. On cloudy nights, clouds reflect heat back toward the surface, keeping temperatures more stable. Most deserts have clear skies for much of the year, which allows heat to leave freely. This is also why desert days are so hot: with few clouds to block it, sunlight reaches the ground directly.

The ground itself plays a role. Sand and bare rock heat up quickly but do not store heat for long. In contrast, areas covered by plants and moist soil warm and cool more slowly, because water must absorb a lot of energy before its temperature changes.

Animals and people living in deserts have adapted to these conditions. Many desert animals are active only at dawn and dusk, when temperatures are moderate, and spend the hottest and coldest hours in burrows. Traditional desert clothing is often loose and layered, protecting the body from the sun by day and holding in warmth after dark.

opts: A large difference between day and night temperatures
